title: Chicken cuts: protein, fat, and calories by part

seo.title: Chicken cuts: protein, fat, and calories by part
seo.meta_description: Chicken breast, thigh, drumstick, and wings do not have the same fat. Compare cooked protein and calories per 100 g and see how much the skin changes the result.
seo.search_intent: Compare the main chicken cuts for protein, fat and calories while separating skin-on from skinless and raw from cooked values.

excerpt: Chicken breast is not the only high-protein part of the bird. Most cuts provide substantial protein, but fat changes much more. Skinless roasted breast is around 31 g protein and 3–4 g fat per 100 g; skin-on wings can approach 18–20 g fat.
content_html:
“Chicken” does not have one nutrition profile. Protein stays fairly high across most cuts, while fat can change several-fold depending on the part and whether the skin is eaten.

A practical cooked comparison per 100 g

CutStateCaloriesProteinFat
BreastMeat only, skinless, roasted~160–170~30–31 g~3–4 g
ThighMeat only, skinless, cooked~200–210~25–27 g~10–11 g
DrumstickMeat only, skinless, cooked~175–190~27–29 g~6–8 g
WingMeat and skin, roasted~250–290~23–27 g~17–20 g

Ranges are more useful than pretending there is one universal number because food-composition entries differ by exact cut, skin, cooking method, and water loss.

Breast stands out for protein relative to fat

A representative skinless roasted breast is about 31 g protein and 3.6 g fat per 100 g. Skinless cooked thigh can be around 26 g protein and 11 g fat.

That is only about 5 g less protein but roughly 7 g more fat per 100 g. The added fat explains much of the roughly 35–50 calorie gap.

Drumstick sits in the middle

Skinless drumstick meat commonly lands around 27–29 g protein and 6–8 g fat per 100 g cooked. It is fattier than breast, but much leaner than a wing served with skin.

This is why lumping every dark-meat cut into one nutrition number is not very helpful.

Skin can change the result substantially

Wings are a clear example because they are often eaten with skin. A roasted skin-on wing reference can approach 18–20 g fat per 100 g — around five times the fat of skinless breast.

Removing the skin lowers fat meaningfully, although it does not make every cut identical to breast because intramuscular fat still differs by part.

Raw and cooked values are not interchangeable

Cooking removes water. If 100 g raw chicken finishes at 75 g, protein and fat become more concentrated per 100 g of the cooked food. A raw entry may show roughly 22–24 g protein/100 g while the cooked version rises above 30 g/100 g without cooking somehow creating protein.

Cooking fat can matter as much as the cut

Ten grams of oil contributes about 90 calories. If a very lean chicken breast retains that amount of added oil, the added energy can exceed the natural calorie difference between several cuts.

For a useful comparison, separate the chicken’s own fat from butter, oil, breading, or sauce added during cooking.

Which cut makes sense?

If the goal is the most protein with the least fat, skinless breast is the simplest choice. Thigh and drumstick provide more fat and often more juiciness while remaining protein-rich. Skin-on wings are substantially more energy-dense at the same weight.

The useful takeaway

Chicken does not have one calorie or fat number. Most cooked cuts provide roughly 25–31 g protein per 100 g, while fat can range from about 3–4 g in skinless breast to 17–20 g in skin-on wings. Always check the cut, skin status, and cooking state.

faq.question: Which chicken cut has the most protein?
faq.answer: Skinless breast is typically among the most concentrated, around 30–31 g protein per 100 g cooked. Other cuts still often provide 25–29 g.

faq.question: Which chicken cut has the least fat?
faq.answer: Skinless breast, at roughly 3–4 g fat per 100 g cooked in representative USDA entries.

faq.question: Does chicken skin add many calories?
faq.answer: It can. Skin concentrates fat; skin-on wings can approach 17–20 g fat per 100 g compared with 3–4 g in skinless breast.
